Stage 3 · Grammar

How much more, exactly?

Anybody can say more positive. The level shows in the word before it.

Read these four sentences.
  • The descriptions were a bit more positive.
  • The descriptions were much more positive.
  • The descriptions were far more positive.
  • Their descriptions weren’t as positive as their friends’.
Which of the first three shows the smallest difference?
Describing something at this level means placing it on a scale, not giving it a label.

She’s tall is an absolute statement, and absolutes are surprisingly unhelpful: tall compared with whom? Most real description in English is comparative. You say how something stands in relation to something else, and the language of comparison is therefore one of the most heavily used systems in the whole level.

English builds comparatives in two ways depending on the length of the adjective. Short adjectives take an ending — tall → taller → the tallest. Longer ones take a separate word — detailed → more detailed → the most detailed. The two systems must never be combined: more taller and most tallest are among the most recognisable errors in learner English. Alongside them sits the equality structure as … as, with its negative not as … as.

What turns a comparison into information is the layer of modifiers on top. She’s taller says almost nothing; She’s slightly taller and She’s far taller say two quite different things, and a listener will take them literally. Far, much, a lot mark a big difference; slightly, a bit, a little mark a small one; by far and easily strengthen a superlative. Note that very cannot do this job: very taller is not English.

One further distinction causes constant trouble and is worth settling now. Fewer counts and less measures. You have fewer wrinkles but less grey hair, because wrinkles are countable and hair is not. Informal spoken English often ignores this; written and examined English does not.

Before you look at the table: the table below gives the forms by syllable count, then the irregulars, then the modifiers. Count the syllables of your adjective before you decide which column you are in.

One more per adjective. Either -er or more, never both: not more taller but taller, not more slimmer but slimmer.

As… as takes as, not than. Not as tall than but as tall as. Than only follows a comparative form.

Not nearly as… as is the strong negative. Not as accurate as means a bit less accurate. Not nearly as accurate as means a great deal less. Learners often reach for very, which does not work here at all.

By far goes before the superlative. By far the most reliable, by far the least accurate. Not the most reliable by far more.

Full grammar reference — comparison — comparatives, superlatives and modifiers

What it is

The full system for placing things on a scale. English forms the comparative with -er or more, the superlative with the … -est or the most, and expresses equality with as … as. On top of that sits a layer of modifiers — far, much, slightly, a bit, nowhere near, by far — that measure how big the difference is.

What it means, and what it does

Description at B1 is mostly comparison. She’s tall gives an absolute; She’s slightly taller than her sister gives a relationship and a scale. When you describe a face, a place or a product, the modifier is what turns a vague impression into information: a bit older, far more detailed and by far the most unusual are three quite different claims.

When and why we use it

She’s tall is an absolute statement, and absolutes are surprisingly unhelpful: tall compared with whom? Most real description in English is comparative. You say how something stands in relation to something else, and the language of comparison is therefore one of the most heavily used systems in the whole level.

English builds comparatives in two ways depending on the length of the adjective. Short adjectives take an ending — tall → taller → the tallest. Longer ones take a separate word — detailed → more detailed → the most detailed. The two systems must never be combined: more taller and most tallest are among the most recognisable errors in learner English. Alongside them sits the equality structure as … as, with its negative not as … as.

What turns a comparison into information is the layer of modifiers on top. She’s taller says almost nothing; She’s slightly taller and She’s far taller say two quite different things, and a listener will take them literally. Far, much, a lot mark a big difference; slightly, a bit, a little mark a small one; by far and easily strengthen a superlative. Note that very cannot do this job: very taller is not English.

One further distinction causes constant trouble and is worth settling now. Fewer counts and less measures. You have fewer wrinkles but less grey hair, because wrinkles are countable and hair is not. Informal spoken English often ignores this; written and examined English does not.

Typical situations

You need comparison for describing people’s appearance, comparing two photographs or two places, discussing changes over time, and any conversation where you weigh two options against each other.

  • Comparing two things — comparative + than.His hair is shorter than it was in the photo.
  • Saying two things are equal — as + adjective + as.She looks as young as her daughter.
  • Saying one is less — not as … as, or less + long adjective.He’s not as well-built as he used to be.
  • Naming the extreme of a group — superlative + the.That’s the most detailed portrait in the room.
  • Measuring a big difference — far, much, a lot + comparative.The second sketch is far more flattering.
  • Measuring a small difference — slightly, a bit, a little + comparative.She’s slightly taller than I remembered.
  • Emphasising a superlative — by far, easily.It’s by far the strangest painting here.
  • Comparing quantities — more / fewer / less + noun.There are fewer details in the background.

How it differs from similar structures

as … as = equal · not as … as = less · not nearly as … as = much less. Choose according to the size of the gap, not at random.
fewer counts individual items · less measures an amount. Fewer wrinkles, less grey hair.

How to build it

Comparative: short adjective + -er + than  ·  more + long adjective + than
Superlative: the + adjective + -est  ·  the most + adjective
Equality: as + adjective + as  ·  not as + adjective + as
Modifier: far / much / a lot / slightly / a bit + comparative  ·  by far + superlative
One syllabletall → taller → the tallest · slim → slimmer → the slimmest
Two syllables in -ycurly → curlier → the curliest · tidy → tidier
Two or more syllablesdetailed → more detailed → the most detailed
Irregulargood → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · little → less → the least
Equalityas mysterious as · not nearly as mysterious as
Negative comparisonless detailed than — used mainly with long adjectives.
QuestionWhich is more old-fashioned, the dress or the hairstyle?
Nounsmore hair · fewer eyelashes · less stubble — fewer counts, less measures.

Spelling and word order

  • One vowel + one consonant doubles the consonant: slim → slimmer, fat → fattest. Not after two vowels: plain → plainer.
  • Consonant + y becomes -ier / -iest: curly → curlier, tidy → tidiest.
  • A silent -e just adds -r / -st: large → larger → the largest.
  • Two-syllable adjectives ending in -er, -ow, -le normally take -er: clever → cleverer, narrow → narrower, simple → simpler.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • than is weak: /ðən/. It is easily confused with then in listening, and the two are frequently swapped in writing.
  • as … as is unstressed at both ends; the stress falls on the adjective: as TALL as.
  • In by far the most, the stress is on far, which is what carries the emphasis.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Never combine the two systems. more taller, most tallest and more better are wrong. Choose -er/-est or more/most, never both.
  • The superlative always takes the, and it is normally followed by a group: the most detailed painting in the room.
  • Very modifies an adjective (very tall) but not a comparative. Use much, far, a lot instead: much taller, never very taller.
  • Fewer goes with countable nouns (fewer eyelashes), less with uncountable (less hair). Informal English often uses less for both, but exams do not accept it.
  • Comparatives can be doubled for a gradual change: His hair is getting greyer and greyer. With long adjectives: more and more detailed.
  • The + comparative … the + comparative links two changes: The older he gets, the quieter he becomes.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • She’s more taller than her sister. → She’s much taller than her sister.Never use more with an -er form.
  • He’s the most old-fashioned of the two. → He’s the more old-fashioned of the two.With exactly two, use the comparative.
  • She looks as young than her daughter. → She looks as young as her daughter.The as … as structure takes as, not than.
  • It’s very more detailed than the sketch. → It’s far more detailed than the sketch.Very cannot modify a comparative.
  • There are less details in the background. → There are fewer details in the background.Details is countable, so fewer.
  • That’s most unusual portrait in the gallery. → That’s the most unusual portrait in the gallery.Superlatives take the.

More examples in context

  • comparativeHis hair is shorter and greyer than it was in the photograph.
  • long adjectiveThe second sketch is more flattering than the first.
  • equalityShe looks almost as young as her daughter.
  • inequalityHe’s not as well-built as he was ten years ago.
  • small differenceShe’s slightly slimmer than in the earlier picture.
  • big differenceThe background is far more detailed than I expected.
  • superlativeIt’s the most mysterious painting in the collection.
  • emphasised superlativeThat’s by far the strangest thing in the room.
  • quantityThere are fewer figures in the foreground and less snow.
  • gradual changeThe older the photograph, the harder it is to recognise her.

A tip for remembering it

Count the syllables first. One syllable, or two ending in -y, takes -er / -est. Anything longer takes more / the most. Then, before you finish the sentence, ask how big is the gap? and put the right modifier in front: far / much for a large one, slightly / a bit for a small one.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Short adjectives take -er / the -est; long ones take more / the most. Never both.
  2. Superlatives always take the, and usually name the group.
  3. As … as for equality; not (nearly) as … as for a gap.
  4. Modify comparatives with far, much, a lot or slightly, a bit — not with very.
  5. Fewer with countable nouns, less with uncountable.
  6. With exactly two items, use the comparative, not the superlative.

9a · Read the whole text first. Then choose the form that fits each gap.

An artist ran a simple experiment. He asked women to describe their own faces to him honestly, and then asked a stranger who had met them for a few minutes to do the same. The two sketches were hung . In almost every case the self-described version was attractive than the stranger’s. One woman described her own face as closed off, and fatter and sadder too. The stranger’s sketch of her was heavy, and the eyes were open. The differences were smaller with the younger participants, but the pattern held. striking result came from the woman who cried when she saw them. Her own description had not been kind as a stranger’s two-minute impression of her.

Stage 5 · Main input

How would you describe them?

Two drawings of the same face, and only one of them looks like a stranger did it.

Before you read: two portraits were drawn of the same face — one from the woman’s own description, one from a stranger’s.

Which do you think looked better?

Decide first. Paragraph B tells you what happened.

How would you describe them?

A forensic artist drew two portraits of the same woman. He never saw her. The difference between the two pictures became one of the most-watched advertisements ever made.

AThe set-up was unusual. A forensic artist — the kind normally employed by the police to draw a suspect from a witness’s description — sat behind a curtain. He could not see the woman on the other side. She described her own face to him: shoulder-length hair, a fringe, a rather large chin. He drew what he heard. Then a stranger who had met her that morning described the same face, and he drew it again.

BThe two portraits were put side by side. Almost every time, the self-described face was older, heavier and sadder than the one the stranger described. One woman had called her own face “a lot more closed off, and fatter, sadder too”. The stranger’s version had softer eyes and a slightly open mouth. The women were shown both drawings together, and several of them cried.

CThe film went round the world within days, and psychologists were quick to point out that it was not an experiment. The women were not chosen at random, the strangers were prompted to be kind, and a commercial company paid for all of it. None of that, though, explains why the film worked. It worked because the gap it showed was one almost everybody recognises: we are far more precise about our own faults than about anybody else’s.

DResearch on self-perception supports the general point, if not the advertisement. People describing themselves use noticeably more negative detail than people describing a stranger. They are also far more specific: a double chin, thin eyebrows, a nose that is slightly crooked. Strangers describe in much broader strokes — blonde, quite slim, well-built, friendly-looking — and rarely mention the features that the person themselves has been thinking about for twenty years.

ESome of this is simply information. You have looked at your own face many thousands of times more often than anyone else has, so you notice smaller changes: the grey coming in, the hair going. A stranger has three seconds and a general impression. It is not that they are being generous. They are working with far less detail, and detail is where dissatisfaction lives.

FThe advertisement ended with a line telling women they were more beautiful than they thought. It is a nice sentiment, and it is also a company selling soap. The more interesting conclusion is smaller and harder to package: the face other people see is not more flattering than yours. It is simply less examined — and by far the most critical description of you that exists anywhere is the one you carry around in your own head.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of the Real Beauty Sketches campaign (2013) and on research into self-perception.
